strengths: Provides a clean theoretical justification (Propositions 1-4) that the proposed self-consistency-based semi-supervised loss is strictly proper, both for posterior-only and joint posterior/likelihood learning settings, extending prior self-consistency work (Schmitt et al., Ivanova et al.) to a new, well-motivated use case.

The core idea of exploiting unlabeled (label-free) data via Bayesian self-consistency to improve robustness under simulation gaps is novel and potentially impactful, since it sidesteps the need for ground-truth parameters on real data, unlike related calibration-based approaches (e.g., Wehenkel et al.).

The illustrative Gaussian normal-means experiment is well-designed as a proof of concept: it isolates the phenomenon of catastrophic posterior collapse/bias under out-of-simulation shift for standard NPE and shows a clear, large, and consistent improvement when adding the self-consistency loss.

Reasonably thorough ablation study over several factors (parameter dimensionality up to 100, size and location of unlabeled dataset, use of summary networks, estimated vs. known likelihood), which helps characterize where the method helps most and where limitations remain (e.g., estimated likelihood, very high dimensions).

Clear, honest discussion of current limitations (reliance on fast density evaluation, difficulties with free-form flows, bias when likelihood is learned) and appropriate positioning relative to related robustness literature.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly self-identifies as 'work in progress' and a 'proof-of-concept,' with only a single, very simple conjugate Gaussian (normal-means) toy model evaluated; no benchmark models with realistic complexity, non-Gaussian/multi-modal posteriors, or actual real-world/misspecified data are tested, despite the abstract's framing around real-world robustness and model misspecification.

Although the introduction and method motivate the approach as enabling training on 'real-world data,' the experiments only ever use synthetic unlabeled data drawn from another Gaussian with shifted mean; no genuine real-data or model-misspecification experiment is performed, so the central practical claim (robustness to real-world data / misspecification) is not actually tested.

No empirical comparison to any of the competing robustness baselines discussed in Related Work (e.g., Gloeckler et al. adversarial robustness, Ward et al./Siahkoohi et al. post hoc corrections, Wehenkel et al. calibration-based approach, Gao et al. generalized Bayesian inference), making it impossible to assess whether the proposed method is actually competitive with existing robustness techniques rather than just outperforming a vanilla NPE baseline.

The conjugate Gaussian setting is an unusually favorable case (closed-form posterior, well-behaved unimodal Gaussian target, exact self-consistency ratio computable), so it is unclear how well results will transfer to more realistic simulators with intractable likelihoods, multimodal or highly correlated posteriors, as the authors themselves note is left to future work.

Rhetorically strong, somewhat unsupported claims such as 'major breakthrough in neural ABI' are not well calibrated to the very limited scope of evidence (one toy model, no real data, no baseline comparisons), which is a significant overclaim relative to the actual empirical support provided.

Practical/computational costs and scalability of the self-consistency loss (need for fast, exact density evaluation, requiring L posterior samples per training step, incompatibility with free-form/flow-matching methods) are only briefly mentioned, without any runtime or scaling analysis, leaving open how burdensome the method is in more realistic settings.

The choice of proposal distribution pC(θ) for the self-consistency variance term is acknowledged as impactful and hard to predict, yet no sensitivity analysis or guidance is given in this paper beyond citing that this is difficult in general.

strengths: The core idea of exploiting Bayesian self-consistency as an unsupervised/semi-supervised regularizer to improve robustness of amortized Bayesian inference under simulation gaps is conceptually appealing and well-motivated.

The paper provides a clean theoretical grounding (Propositions 1-4) showing that the self-consistency loss and the combined semi-supervised loss are strictly proper, which gives some principled justification for why the approach should not introduce bias asymptotically.

The experimental results on the toy normal-means model are visually compelling and show a stark qualitative difference between standard NPE (which collapses/becomes badly biased out-of-distribution) and NPE+SC (which remains accurate far outside the training region).

The ablations (dimensionality, size/mean of unlabeled data, known vs. estimated likelihood, with/without summary network) provide some systematic exploration of the method's sensitivity within the single toy setting.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly self-identifies as a 'proof-of-concept' and 'work in progress,' with a boxed disclaimer stating that further experiments on other model classes, challenging posterior geometries, and high dimensions are left to a 'full version.' This is a strong indicator that the submission is incomplete for a top-tier venue and evaluation is insufficient to support the claims made.

All empirical evidence comes from a single, highly idealized conjugate Gaussian ('normal means') toy model with a closed-form posterior. There is no evaluation on any standard SBI benchmark (e.g., SIR, Lotka-Volterra, or the models used in the very robustness papers cited), nor any real-world or genuinely misspecified data, despite the abstract's claim that the method works with data 'originating from any source, including real-world data.'

The central claims are dramatically overstated relative to the evidence: phrases like 'major breakthrough in neural ABI' and 'no existing ABI approach achieves similar degrees of robustness' are asserted based on one synthetic toy example, without any direct empirical comparison to the competing robustness methods discussed in Section 3 (e.g., Gloeckler et al., Ward et al., Wehenkel et al., Gao et al.). No baseline other than plain NPE is benchmarked quantitatively.

The theoretical contribution (Propositions 1-4) is a relatively straightforward extension/restatement of properties already established in the cited prior work on self-consistency losses (Ivanova et al. 2024; Schmitt et al. 2024); the genuinely novel element is mainly the combination with unlabeled/out-of-simulation data, which is not itself analyzed theoretically (e.g., no theory bounding bias reduction as a function of the unlabeled data's proximity to the OOD test point, no analysis of failure modes at 100D or under likelihood misspecification, where results already degrade).

The 100-dimensional and estimated-likelihood settings show visibly larger residual bias, but this is not analyzed or discussed in depth; the paper does not explore why the method's benefits shrink in these more realistic conditions, which are precisely the conditions of most practical interest.

The unlabeled data in the experiment is itself simulated from a shifted Gaussian with a known analytic form (Eq. 14), i.e., it is not real-world data and its distributional shift is fully controlled and well-behaved; this undercuts the claim of robustness to 'model misspecification' with genuinely unstructured real-world observations.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, and while hyperparameters are listed, there is no information on variance/uncertainty of results across repeated training runs (error bars in figures appear to reflect variability but this is not clearly described), nor sensitivity to choice of pC(θ), which the authors themselves note 'can influence training dynamics considerably' in a way 'difficult to anticipate.'

The related-work comparison is only qualitative (a bullet list of conceptual differences) rather than empirical, making it impossible to assess whether the proposed method actually outperforms competing robustness approaches in practice.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and well-recognized problem: the poor pre-asymptotic robustness of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) under simulation gaps/model misspecification.

The core idea of using Bayesian self-consistency losses on unlabeled (real or otherwise out-of-simulation) data to regularize posterior approximators is conceptually elegant and, to my knowledge, not previously explored in this form.

Solid theoretical grounding: the paper provides clean proofs that the self-consistency loss (and the combined semi-supervised loss) is strictly proper, which is a meaningful theoretical guarantee showing no trade-off between the two loss terms at the population level.

Compared favorably positioned against existing robustness approaches (Gloeckler et al., Ward et al., Siahkoohi et al., Wehenkel et al.): it needs no labeled calibration data, no post hoc correction step, and preserves full amortized inference speed at test time.

The single case study (multivariate Gaussian normal-means model) is examined with a reasonably thorough set of ablations (dimensionality up to 100, size and location of unlabeled data, known vs. estimated likelihood, with/without summary network), giving some insight into when/why the method helps or struggles.
Clear and honest writing, including an explicit acknowledgment of the preliminary nature of the work.
weaknesses: The paper is explicitly and self-admittedly a 'proof-of-concept'/'work in progress' with only a single, very simple synthetic experiment (Gaussian normal-means model with a closed-form conjugate posterior). This is far short of the empirical rigor expected at a top-tier venue, and the authors themselves state that further verification across model classes, posterior geometries, and dimensionalities is left to a 'full version.'

No experiments on real-world data are presented, despite the central motivating claim that the method enables training on 'unlabeled data originating from any source, including real-world data.' The unlabeled set in the experiments is itself synthetic (drawn from a shifted Gaussian), so the practical claim about real-world robustness is untested.

No empirical comparison against any of the competing robustness methods discussed in Related Work (e.g., Gloeckler et al.'s adversarial regularization, Ward et al.'s post hoc correction, Wehenkel et al.'s calibration-based approach). The only baseline is standard NPE without self-consistency, which makes it impossible to assess whether the proposed method is actually competitive with, rather than merely superior to a weak baseline in a favorable toy setting.

The method requires access to (or joint learning of) the likelihood p(x|θ), which is often unavailable or intractable in genuine simulation-based inference settings that motivate ABI in the first place; the experiments with an estimated likelihood already show noticeably worse performance (especially in posterior SD bias), suggesting the practically relevant likelihood-free case is less convincing.
Degradation is already visible at 100 parameter dimensions in the toy experiment, raising doubts about scalability to realistic high-dimensional models common in modern SBI applications.

The rhetorical framing ('a major breakthrough in neural ABI') is considerably stronger than what a single low-dimensional synthetic conjugate-Gaussian example can support; such claims should be tempered until broader validation is available.

No analysis of computational overhead introduced by the self-consistency loss (which requires L additional posterior samples and density evaluations per training step), nor of sensitivity to the choice of proposal distribution pC(θ), which the authors themselves note 'can influence training dynamics considerably' in unpredictable ways.
No comparison of alternative self-consistency scores C, or ablation of the trade-off weight λ in Eq. (3), leaving open how sensitive results are to these design choices.

As a conjugate Gaussian model, the case study essentially gives the self-consistency loss access to a very informative, well-behaved likelihood signal exactly matching the analytic posterior family, which may make the method's success here a best-case scenario unlikely to generalize to more complex posterior geometries (multimodality, funnels) that the authors mention only as future work.

strengths: Addresses an important and well-recognized problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference under model misspecification / out-of-simulation data.

Elegant theoretical extension of self-consistency losses (Schmitt et al. 2024) to a semi-supervised setting that incorporates unlabeled (potentially real) data without requiring ground-truth parameters.
Clean theoretical results (Propositions 1-4) establishing strict properness of the self-consistency loss and its combination with standard simulation-based losses, with reasonably rigorous proofs.

Includes both a controlled synthetic case study (multivariate normal) with an analytic reference posterior and a real-world case study (air passenger traffic) benchmarked against a gold-standard MCMC (Stan) sampler.

Reasonably thorough ablations in the synthetic case study across dimensionality, unlabeled dataset size, distributional shift magnitude, presence of summary networks, and known vs. estimated likelihoods.
Method requires no post-hoc correction and preserves full amortization/inference speed, which is a practical advantage over some competing robustness approaches.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly frames its results as preliminary ("initial experiments") and hedges its central claim ("If our findings also generalize... we believe... major breakthrough"), which is an unusual and somewhat concerning admission for a paper aiming to substantiate a strong contribution claim.

Empirical validation is narrow: only two case studies, both with relatively simple, low-dimensional, tractable-likelihood models (Gaussian means, linear autoregressive model); no complex/mechanistic simulators typical of real ABI applications are tested.

No direct empirical comparison against the closest competing methods discussed in related work (e.g., Wehenkel et al. 2024, Gloeckler et al. 2023, Ward et al. 2022); comparisons remain purely qualitative/conceptual.

The core practical scenario of interest (unknown/intractable likelihood) is only lightly explored, and the paper's own results show markedly worse performance (especially posterior SD bias) when the likelihood must be estimated jointly, undermining applicability to genuinely simulation-based/likelihood-free settings.
Sensitivity to the choice of proposal distribution pC(θ) is flagged as important but not systematically studied beyond using the prior.

Very small unlabeled sample sizes in the real-data case study (M=4,8,15 countries) and no reported variability (e.g., multiple seeds/runs, confidence intervals) for the reported metrics, limiting confidence in the robustness of the claimed gains.

The air-traffic case study still uses a known/tractable Gaussian likelihood, so it does not truly stress-test the more realistic likelihood-free scenario despite being framed as a "real-world" validation.
Discussion and abstract language (e.g., "major breakthrough") overstate the significance relative to the modest, narrow-scope evidence presented.

strengths: The core idea of combining strictly-proper simulation-based losses with a Bayesian self-consistency loss on unlabeled (potentially real) data is conceptually elegant and well-motivated, addressing a genuine and important weakness of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI): poor pre-asymptotic behavior on out-of-simulation data.

The paper provides formal propositions (with proofs in the appendix) establishing strict properness of the proposed semi-supervised loss, giving some theoretical grounding for why the method should recover the true posterior at the global optimum.

Two case studies are included: a controlled synthetic normal-means problem with an analytic reference posterior, and a real-world autoregressive air-passenger-traffic model compared against Stan/MCMC, which together provide at least a qualitative demonstration that the method can help.

The normal-means experiments include multiple ablation-style analyses (dimensionality, amount of unlabeled data, distance of unlabeled data from training data, known vs. estimated likelihood, with/without summary network), giving some insight into what drives the improvement.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly hedges its central claims ("results of our initial experiments," "if our findings also generalize to other scenarios and model classes, we believe... a major breakthrough"), which signals that the work is preliminary and not yet validated broadly enough to support the strong rhetoric used elsewhere in the paper (e.g., "we believe... is a major breakthrough in neural ABI"). This is a significant mismatch between claims and evidence.

No empirical comparison against any of the competing robustness methods discussed at length in Related Work (Gloeckler et al. adversarial regularization, Ward et al./Siahkoohi et al. post hoc correction, Gao et al. generalized Bayesian inference, Wehenkel et al. calibration-based correction). Without such baselines, it is impossible to assess whether the proposed method is actually better, comparable, or worse than existing robustness techniques.

The real-world case study is small in scale (15 countries, a simple AR(1) model with 5 parameters) and the self-consistency loss is evaluated on very few unlabeled real observations (M=4, 8, 15 countries), raising concerns about how well conclusions generalize to more complex, higher-dimensional real-world simulators where model misspecification is typically more severe and less easily corrected by a handful of consistency constraints.

The method's strongest results rely on a known analytic likelihood; when the likelihood must be estimated jointly (the realistic scenario for most simulators used in ABI), the paper itself acknowledges considerably worse performance (posterior SD bias, MMD), undermining the generality of the claimed robustness gains.

The theoretical contribution is an incremental extension of prior self-consistency work (Schmitt et al. 2024; Ivanova et al. 2024), essentially applying a known loss to a new (unlabeled/real-data) setting rather than introducing fundamentally new machinery; the propositions largely restate known properness arguments.

The paper notes that the choice of proposal distribution pC(θ) for the self-consistency variance term "can influence training dynamics considerably, with empirical consequences being difficult to anticipate," but this sensitivity is not systematically studied, leaving a key practical hyperparameter unexplored.

No computational overhead/runtime analysis is provided for the added self-consistency loss (e.g., cost of L additional density evaluations per training step), despite amortization speed being a central selling point of ABI methods.

No discussion of variance across random seeds/multiple training runs for the main comparisons (only error bars across factor levels in appendix figures), leaving uncertainty about the robustness/reproducibility of the reported gains.

The experimental design intentionally varies factors one-at-a-time due to "combinatorial explosion" concerns, but this leaves open whether the method holds up under realistic combinations of high dimensionality, small unlabeled datasets, and estimated likelihoods simultaneously — arguably the most relevant setting for real applications.

strengths: Solid theoretical contribution: the paper proves (Propositions 1-4) that self-consistency losses based on the Bayesian self-consistency ratio are strictly proper, and that combining them additively with a standard simulation-based loss preserves strict properness for any choice of unlabeled data distribution p*(x). This gives a principled no-trade-off guarantee between the two loss terms.

The proposed semi-supervised scheme is conceptually appealing: it does not require ground-truth parameters for the unlabeled/real data (unlike Wehenkel et al.), requires no post-hoc correction or architecture modification at inference time (preserving amortized inference speed), and works even with as few as one or four unlabeled observations.

The normal-means experiments (Section 4.1, Figures 1 and 3-4) provide a clean, interpretable demonstration where the analytic posterior is known, allowing precise quantification of bias and MMD; the method shows large robustness gains that persist across dimensionality (up to 100D), unlabeled dataset size, and observation location, including with an estimated (rather than known) likelihood.

The real-world air passenger traffic case study (Section 4.2) with Stan as a gold-standard reference is a valuable addition, showing that the approach can substantially reduce posterior bias/Wasserstein distance relative to Stan on real, moderately complex regression data with covariates, not just synthetic misspecification scenarios.

The paper is generally clearly written with formal definitions, useful appendix details on architectures/training, and reasonably thorough ablations over multiple factors (dimensionality, M, mean shift, summary network, likelihood type).
weaknesses: The method fundamentally relies on evaluating (or approximating) the likelihood p(x*|θ) for the self-consistency loss. This is a substantial limitation for the many ABI/SBI applications with genuinely intractable likelihoods (the primary motivating use case for neural ABI); the paper's own ablation shows accuracy degrades notably when the likelihood must be estimated, and this limitation is not thoroughly discussed or resolved.

No empirical comparison against the competing robustness methods discussed in Related Work (Gloeckler et al. 2023 adversarial regularization, Ward et al. 2022 / Siahkoohi et al. 2023 post-hoc corrections, Wehenkel et al. 2024 calibration-set approach, Gao et al. 2023 generalized Bayesian inference). Only vanilla NPE is used as a baseline, making it hard to judge whether the proposed method's robustness gains are competitive with, or superior to, existing alternatives.

Experimental scope is narrow: only two case studies (a synthetic Gaussian conjugate model and one real-world AR(1) regression model with 5 parameters), both with fairly simple/tractable likelihood structures. This is insufficient to support the abstract/discussion's characterization of the method as a potential 'major breakthrough' in neural ABI; the paper itself hedges this claim as contingent on future generalization, which is an unusually strong claim for such limited empirical evidence.

Potential methodological ambiguity in the real-data case study: in the M=15 setting (Table 3), the self-consistency loss appears to be trained on data from all 15 countries that are also used for final evaluation, raising questions about train/test overlap and whether the reported improvements partly reflect fitting on evaluation data rather than genuine out-of-sample generalization; this is not clearly addressed in the text.

The method is explicitly stated to be incompatible with free-form flow-matching approaches (due to reliance on fast density evaluation), restricting applicability to normalizing-flow-based posterior/likelihood estimators, which somewhat limits generality relative to modern SBI toolchains.

Sensitivity to the choice of proposal distribution pC(θ) for the self-consistency variance term is acknowledged as impactful on training dynamics but not systematically studied in the experiments, leaving an important design choice under-explored.

No analysis of computational overhead (training time, convergence behavior) introduced by the additional self-consistency loss term relative to standard NPE training, nor of variance/uncertainty of results across multiple training seeds/replications.

strengths: Addresses an important, well-motivated problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) under simulation gap / out-of-distribution observations, which is a recognized limitation of NPE-type methods.

Clean theoretical contribution: strict properness of the self-consistency loss and of the combined semi-supervised loss (Propositions 1-4) is proven, and importantly it is shown there is no trade-off between the standard simulation-based loss and the self-consistency loss regardless of whether the unlabeled data distribution matches the training distribution.

The method is practically appealing: it requires no ground-truth labels for the unlabeled/real data, no post-hoc correction, no loss of amortization, and adds no significant computational overhead at inference time.

Diverse and reasonably realistic set of case studies (toy Gaussian, real-world air passenger traffic with Stan gold-standard comparison, high-dimensional Hodgkin-Huxley time series, and MNIST image denoising), spanning different data modalities (tabular, time series, images) and both known/analytic and estimated likelihoods.

Extensive ablations in the toy Gaussian model (dimensionality, size of unlabeled data, distance of unlabeled data from training distribution, summary network vs. not, known vs. estimated likelihood) that support the claimed robustness mechanism.

Results consistently show large, sometimes dramatic, improvements over standard NPE baselines across all case studies, including quantitative metrics (MMD, Wasserstein distance, bias) and qualitative visualizations.

Reasonable related work discussion positioning the contribution relative to adversarial robustness training, post-hoc correction, and calibration-based approaches, with clear articulation of the distinguishing properties of this method.
weaknesses: The empirical benefit critically depends on the availability of unlabeled real/OOD data at training time that is at least somewhat representative of the eventual OOD region; the toy experiment shows that if the unlabeled data mean equals the labeled data mean (µ*=0), the method offers no protection, and there is no systematic study of how gracefully the method degrades when unlabeled data location does not match or barely overlaps the actual OOD test region encountered at deployment (real-world evaluation cannot guarantee such information is available a priori).

Limited baseline comparisons against other robustness methods for ABI mentioned in Related Work (e.g., Gloeckler et al. adversarial regularization, Wehenkel et al. calibration-set approach, Huang et al. robust statistics) — the paper only compares against vanilla NPE, making it hard to assess how the method's robustness/accuracy trade-off compares to existing alternatives.

The strict properness claim (Proposition 4, and the general framework) is explicitly stated to fail when both posterior and likelihood are approximate simultaneously (the MNIST NPLE case), which is precisely the most challenging and highlighted setting empirically; the paper acknowledges this only briefly and does not analyze how far from the theoretical guarantee the joint learning may end up in practice, weakening the link between theory and the most complex experiment.

The method's applicability is stated to be limited to density estimators with efficient likelihood evaluation (e.g., normalizing flows), explicitly excluding increasingly popular free-form generative approaches like flow matching or diffusion models, which restricts the scope/impact of the contribution given current trends in the field.

Sensitivity of training dynamics to the choice of proposal distribution pC(θ) for the variance-based consistency loss is noted as an important and difficult-to-anticipate factor, but the paper does not provide practical guidance, hyperparameter search, or robustness analysis regarding this choice beyond the simple toy model.

The real-world air-traffic case study lacks a truly independent OOD real-world evaluation (both labeled and self-consistency data derive from the same Eurostat dataset/domain), so the demonstration of robustness against genuine model misspecification with real data is less rigorous than the synthetic and semi-synthetic studies.

No wall-clock or computational overhead comparison is given for the additional self-consistency loss term during training (only inference speed is claimed to be preserved, which is trivially true since it doesn't affect the trained network's forward pass), making it hard to assess the practical training cost of the method, especially with L samples per iteration for variance estimation.

Some claims in the abstract/introduction (e.g., 'robust ABI for widespread and safe application', 'inference remains accurate even far from training data') are somewhat strong relative to the fairly small-scale, low-dimensional-parameter-count case studies (except the parameter dimensionality ablation in the toy model), leaving open questions about scalability to more complex, higher-dimensional real scientific models.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated problem: the fragility of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) under simulation gaps/model misspecification.

The theoretical framing (Propositions 1-4) is clearly presented and gives some formal justification for why the self-consistency loss is strictly proper and can be safely combined with the standard simulation-based loss without introducing a trade-off.

The experimental scope is broad, spanning a controlled toy Gaussian model, a real-world autoregressive time-series application (air traffic), a high-dimensional ODE-based neuroscience model (Hodgkin-Huxley), and an image denoising task (MNIST), which speaks to some generality of the approach.

The method is simple to add on top of existing normalizing-flow-based NPE/NPLE pipelines and does not require ground-truth parameters for the unlabeled data, nor does it sacrifice amortized inference speed at test time.
weaknesses: The core self-consistency loss machinery is taken essentially unchanged from prior work (Schmitt et al. 2024, Ivanova et al. 2024); the main contribution here is applying it to unlabeled/out-of-distribution data in a semi-supervised setting. This is a relatively incremental extension, and the theoretical propositions largely restate/trivially combine known properness results (e.g., Proposition 3 is a one-line consequence of additivity of proper losses).

No empirical comparison is made against any of the directly competing robustness methods discussed in Related Work (Gloeckler et al. adversarial regularization, Ward et al. and Siahkoohi et al. post-hoc corrections, Wehenkel et al. calibration-set approach, Gao et al. generalized Bayesian inference). The paper only argues qualitatively why its approach is preferable, without any quantitative head-to-head evaluation, which makes the claimed advantages unsubstantiated.

In three of the four case studies (normal model, Hodgkin-Huxley, MNIST) the 'unlabeled data' is not actually real-world data but synthetic data generated from a deliberately shifted parameter distribution controlled by the experimenter. This undercuts the paper's central narrative and abstract claim of leveraging 'unlabeled data originating from any source, including real data' — only the air traffic case study uses genuine real-world unlabeled data.

The robustness claims appear sensitive to the specific relationship between the self-consistency training distribution and the evaluation distribution. Appendix Figure 6 shows that merely having self-consistency data at μ*=1 (only slightly shifted from training) fixes performance uniformly across all tested μobs up to 11, which is a very strong extrapolation claim that is not stress-tested for more complex or multi-directional distribution shifts, nor is it clear whether the MMD metric is fully capturing calibration quality versus simply preventing variance collapse.

The MNIST denoising case study includes no quantitative metrics at all (e.g., no calibration statistics, coverage, or divergence measures) — only qualitative visual comparisons of a handful of images, which is a weak form of evidence for a paper making strong robustness claims.

The sensitivity of the method to the choice of proposal distribution pC(θ) for the self-consistency variance is acknowledged as being 'difficult to anticipate' but is not systematically studied; only prior-based proposals are used in the experiments, leaving an important design choice underexplored.

The stated limitation that the method requires fast density evaluation (excluding flow-matching and diffusion-based estimators, which are increasingly standard in modern ABI) meaningfully limits the applicability of the proposed approach going forward.

No analysis of the added computational overhead of the self-consistency loss (extra proposal samples, extra likelihood/density evaluations per training step) is provided, despite the claim that the approach 'retains ABI's characteristic speed.'

Architectures and problem scales used in experiments are relatively small (e.g., simple spline flows, LSTM summary networks, CPU-only training in three of four case studies), raising questions about scalability to more complex/higher-dimensional real-world Bayesian inference problems that motivate ABI in the first place.

strengths: Extends self-consistency losses (previously used for training efficiency) to a new and important problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference under simulation gaps/model misspecification, which is a well-motivated and timely contribution.

Provides clean theoretical results (Propositions 1-4) proving strict properness of the self-consistency loss and showing that adding it to a standard simulation-based loss introduces no trade-off, holding regardless of whether the unlabeled data distribution matches the model.

Empirical evaluation spans four diverse and increasingly realistic settings: a controllable Gaussian toy model, a real-world autoregressive air-traffic forecasting model benchmarked against Stan (gold-standard MCMC), a high-dimensional Hodgkin-Huxley neuroscience simulator, and MNIST image denoising with implicit prior/likelihood networks -- demonstrating broad applicability.

Thorough ablations in the toy model (parameter dimensionality up to 100, size of unlabeled data down to M=4, distance of unlabeled data from training distribution, presence of summary network, estimated vs. analytic likelihood) that consistently support the core claims.

Method does not require ground-truth parameters for unlabeled/real data, does not sacrifice amortized inference speed at test time, and does not need adversarial training or post-hoc corrections, differentiating it favorably from several cited alternatives.

Demonstrates practically meaningful robustness gains with very small amounts of unlabeled data (as few as 4 real observations), which is appealing for real scientific applications where labeled calibration data is unavailable.
weaknesses: No direct empirical comparison against the closest related methods (e.g., Wehenkel et al.'s calibration-set approach, Gloeckler et al.'s adversarial robustness, Ward et al./Siahkoohi et al.'s post-hoc corrections); differences are only discussed qualitatively in Related Work, weakening claims of comparative advantage.

The method fundamentally requires fast, tractable density evaluation (e.g., normalizing flows) and is explicitly acknowledged to be impractical for increasingly popular free-form generative models such as flow matching or diffusion-based posterior/likelihood estimators, limiting general applicability.

The self-consistency loss requires access to a (possibly approximate) likelihood; while the paper shows results with an estimated likelihood, this still assumes a jointly learnable likelihood network, which may not be feasible in fully simulation-based/likelihood-free settings without additional density estimation overhead.

The influence of the proposal distribution pC(θ) used in the self-consistency variance term is noted as potentially impactful on training dynamics but is not systematically explored beyond using the prior as default.

The MNIST denoising case study's misspecification scenario is somewhat artificially constructed (synthetically removing prior blur for the unlabeled set), which, while illustrative, provides weaker evidence of real-world applicability compared to the air-traffic case study.
Claims that the approach 'retains ABI's characteristic speed' are asserted but not directly quantified with wall-clock inference/training time comparisons in the main results.

Evaluation relies mainly on MMD/Wasserstein/bias metrics with a modest number of refits (10); calibration diagnostics (e.g., simulation-based calibration) that are standard in the ABI robustness literature are not reported, leaving calibration quality only indirectly assessed.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated extension of Bayesian self-consistency losses (previously used for simulation efficiency) to a semi-supervised setting that leverages unlabeled real-world data to improve ABI robustness under model misspecification/domain shift.

Solid theoretical contribution: rigorous proofs (Propositions 1-4) showing the self-consistency loss is strictly proper and, crucially, that combining it with standard simulation-based NPE losses introduces no trade-off, since both target the same analytic posterior—distinguishing this approach from prior regularization-based robustness methods.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation across four case studies (toy multivariate normal, real-world air traffic forecasting with Stan as gold-standard reference, high-dimensional Hodgkin-Huxley neuroscience time series, and MNIST image denoising), demonstrating consistent and often dramatic robustness gains.

Strong baseline comparisons, including NPE-DANN, NPE-MMD, NNPE, VAE, online-trained NPE, and Schmitt et al. (2024)'s supervised self-consistency variant, showing the proposed method's clear superiority under prior/model misspecification.

Demonstrates practical efficiency and low data requirements—robustness gains achieved with as few as 4 unlabeled observations, and speed of amortized inference is preserved (no architecture modification post-training).

Thorough reproducibility support: detailed appendices with hyperparameters, architectures, computational resources, and code availability; useful FAQ section addressing many practical/motivational questions a reviewer might raise.
weaknesses: The strict-properness guarantee formally requires a known (or at least separately well-estimated) likelihood; when both posterior and likelihood are jointly learned (the more common SBI scenario with implicit simulators), the theoretical guarantee breaks down, and the paper's own experiments show degraded performance (particularly in posterior SD bias) in this estimated-likelihood setting.

The method's reliance on fast, exact density evaluation restricts its applicability to flow-based density estimators and precludes use with increasingly popular free-form generative models (flow matching, diffusion-based samplers), a significant limitation acknowledged only briefly as future work.

Practical training required ad hoc stabilization tricks (loss weight λ scheduling/warm-up, numerical instability issues at initialization), suggesting the method is less of a plug-and-play addition than the theory implies.

No direct empirical comparison to Wehenkel et al. (2024), explicitly described as the closest related work, despite differing assumptions (labeled calibration set) that would make for an informative baseline.

The MNIST 'image denoising' task, while illustrative of higher-dimensional applicability, is a synthetic blurring simulation rather than a genuinely real-world imaging problem, somewhat overstating the 'real-world case studies' framing in the abstract.

Ablations on the choice of self-consistency score C (only variance-based ratio explored) and the proposal distribution pC(θ) are relatively limited, leaving open how sensitive results are to these design choices.
Computational overhead/training time comparisons between NPE and NPE+SC are not clearly quantified, making it harder to assess the practical cost of adding the self-consistency loss.

strengths: Solid theoretical contribution: the paper proves that Bayesian self-consistency losses are strictly proper (Propositions 1-4) and that combining them with standard simulation-based NPE losses introduces no trade-off in the training objective, which is a meaningful and non-trivial extension of Schmitt et al. (2024) from a data-efficiency tool to a robustness tool.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation across four case studies of increasing complexity: a controllable toy multivariate Gaussian model, a real-world autoregressive air-traffic forecasting model with real covariates, a high-dimensional Hodgkin-Huxley neuroscience simulator, and an MNIST image denoising task, showing consistent robustness gains.

Comparisons against a reasonably broad set of relevant baselines/alternatives (standard NPE, NPE-DANN, NPE-MMD, NNPE, VAE, online-trained NPE, and Schmitt et al. 2024's SC loss on simulated data), with the proposed method outperforming all of them under prior/model misspecification.

The method preserves full amortization and inference speed (no post-hoc correction, no architecture change at test time), and does not require ground-truth parameters for unlabeled/real data, distinguishing it from competing robustness approaches such as Wehenkel et al. (2024).

Good reproducibility practices: detailed appendices with architectures, hyperparameters, priors, and compute resources for every experiment, plus a thorough FAQ section addressing many natural reader questions about design choices (e.g., choice of proposal distribution, weighting schedule).
weaknesses: The method's practical scope is significantly narrower than the framing suggests: most of the strongest robustness results (normal model, air-traffic model) rely on an assumed *known/analytic* likelihood, which is atypical for genuine simulation-based inference (where likelihood intractability is usually the very reason ABI/NPE is used in the first place). When the likelihood must itself be estimated (Hodgkin-Huxley, MNIST), the paper's own results show noticeably degraded bias and calibration, undermining the central robustness claim in the more realistic intractable-likelihood regime.

The approach is restricted to density estimators with fast, exact likelihood evaluation (e.g., normalizing flows), explicitly excluding increasingly popular free-form generative architectures such as flow matching and diffusion models; this is acknowledged as a limitation but substantially limits the method's applicability to the current SOTA ABI toolchain.

Proposition 4 shows that when both posterior and likelihood are unknown, the self-consistency loss alone admits degenerate global minimizers (e.g., q(θ|x)=p(θ), q(x|θ)∝1); the paper argues this is resolved by coupling with the simulation-based loss, but no formal guarantee is given for the *joint* minimizer's correctness in this more realistic dual-unknown setting beyond empirical evidence.

The 'unlabeled' data used for self-consistency in several experiments is still synthetic/simulated from a shifted distribution (multivariate normal, Hodgkin-Huxley) rather than truly independent real observations, and even in the real-data experiments (air traffic, MNIST) the setup is relatively controlled (small number of covariates/countries, single-digit-class MNIST subset), leaving open how well the approach scales to more complex, higher-dimensional, or multimodal real-world posteriors.

The self-consistency loss is estimated from very small unlabeled sample sizes (M as low as 1-32) using a variance-based estimator; the paper does not thoroughly analyze the statistical variance/bias of this finite-sample SC loss estimate itself, which could be an important source of instability not fully explored beyond ad hoc λ scheduling.

While speed preservation at inference time is argued, the paper provides limited quantitative benchmarking of the added training-time overhead (extra density evaluations across L consistency samples per batch) relative to standard NPE training, despite claiming the method 'preserves ABI's characteristic speed.'

The MNIST denoising task, while presented as 'high-dimensional,' is restricted to a single digit class ('0'), which is a fairly narrow and simplified generative task relative to the natural image complexity ABI methods would need to handle in more realistic applications.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and important problem: robustness of amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) under simulation gaps/model misspecification, which is a major barrier to safe real-world deployment of ABI methods.

The core theoretical contribution (Propositions 1-4) is clean and well-presented: self-consistency losses are shown to be strictly proper and, crucially, to target the same analytic posterior as standard simulation-based losses, so combining them in a semi-supervised objective introduces no trade-off. This distinguishes the method conceptually from prior robustness approaches that implicitly alter the target distribution (e.g., regularization or domain-adaptation methods).

The method is simple to implement, requires no post-hoc correction or loss of amortization at inference time, and does not require ground-truth parameters for the unlabeled/real data, which is a genuine practical advantage over related work such as Wehenkel et al. (2024).

Empirical validation is extensive and spans a good range of complexity: a controllable toy Gaussian model with an analytic posterior for precise error quantification, a real-world autoregressive time-series model benchmarked against Stan/MCMC, a high-dimensional Hodgkin-Huxley ODE model, and a high-dimensional MNIST image denoising task with a jointly learned likelihood -- collectively showing the method generalizes across data modalities and model classes.

The paper includes non-trivial ablations (parameter dimensionality up to 100, unlabeled dataset size as small as 4, known vs. estimated likelihood, with/without summary network) and comparisons against alternative robustness baselines (NPE-MMD, NPE-DANN, NNPE, VAE, and Schmitt et al. 2024's supervised SC variant), consistently showing the proposed semi-supervised SC approach outperforms these alternatives under misspecification.

The appendix is unusually thorough, providing full proofs, an FAQ addressing likely reviewer questions (e.g., choice of proposal distribution, weighting hyperparameter, why couple SC with NPE loss despite strict properness), and detailed experimental/architecture settings that support reproducibility.
The method preserves the key practical benefit of ABI (fast amortized inference) since no architecture modification or iterative correction is needed at test time.
weaknesses: The known-likelihood assumption is central to the strongest theoretical guarantees (Proposition 1), and results degrade noticeably when the likelihood must be estimated (as shown in Appendix D, Figure 7 top row); this limits applicability to genuinely likelihood-free/simulation-based inference settings where neither likelihood nor posterior is known, which is arguably the primary use case for ABI/SBI.

The method's compatibility with free-form generative modeling approaches (flow matching, diffusion) is explicitly noted as an open limitation, restricting the applicability of the approach to density-evaluable architectures (normalizing flows) at a time when free-form generative models are increasingly popular in SBI.

The choice and sensitivity of the self-consistency weight λ and the proposal distribution pC(θ) (posterior vs. prior) are handled somewhat heuristically (via FAQ discussion and a linear warm-up schedule for high-dimensional cases) rather than through a systematic ablation or principled selection procedure, despite the paper's claim that λ 'does not control a trade-off'.

Real-world case studies (air traffic, MNIST) do not have fully independent ground truth for the SC-loss unlabeled evaluation data in the same way the toy model does, so the degree of genuine domain shift/misspecification tested is less rigorously controlled outside of the synthetic Gaussian experiment.

The comparison to prior robustness methods (NPE-MMD, NPE-DANN, NNPE) is conducted only on the low-dimensional Gaussian toy case, not on the more complex real-world case studies, leaving open whether the reported large margins of improvement hold for higher-dimensional or real data settings.

The paper could more clearly discuss computational overhead of the SC loss (extra density evaluations, variance estimation over L posterior samples) relative to standard NPE training, particularly for high-dimensional problems like the image denoising task.
